label: intersection lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
The composition of the corestriction and restriction maps is multiplication by $[G:H]$ on each $H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$.
Since $\text{gcd}([G:H],p)=1$, the composition is an isomorphism on each $H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$.
We conclude that $\text{res}:H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)\to H^*(H,\mathbb{F}_p)$ is an injective ring map and each $\text{cor}^d:H^d(H,\mathbb{F}_p)\to H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$ is a surjective group homomorphism.

View $H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$ as a subring of $H^*(H,\mathbb{F}_p)$ via restriction.
If $u\in I(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$, then $\text{res}(u)\in I(H,\mathbb{F}_p)$ by \cite[Proposition 2.3(1)]{GM}.
Thus
\begin{equation*}
    I(G,\mathbb{F}_p)\subset H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)\cap I(H,\mathbb{F}_p).
\end{equation*}
If $v\in H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)\cap H^d(H,\mathbb{F}_p)_{\text{neg}}$, then $v=\text{res}(u)$ for some $u\in H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$.
We have $\text{cor}^d(v)=\text{cor}^d(\text{res}^d(u))=[G:H]u$ is an element of $H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)_{\text{neg}}$ by Lemma \ref{lemma:corestriction}.
We conclude that $u$ is an element of $H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)_{\text{neg}}$ since $[G:H]$ is invertible in $H^d(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$.
For an inhomogeneous $w\in H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)\cap I(H,\mathbb{F}_p)$, perform the above procedure on each homogeneous piece.
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
    I(G,\mathbb{F}_p)\supset H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)\cap I(H,\mathbb{F}_p). \qedhere
\end{equation*}

label: index 2 subgroups
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{index 2 subgroups}
Let $G$ be a finite 2-group that is not elementary abelian and $F$ a field.
Assume that the restriction of $u\in H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)$ is eventually negligible over $F$ in the cohomology of each index 2 subgroup of $G$.
Then $u$ is eventually negligible in $H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)$ over $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the squaring map is linear in the ring $H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)$, it is sufficient to check the claim on homogeneous $u$.
Denote by $H_i$ the index 2 subgroups of $G$ for $1\leq i\leq n$.
Let $V$ be a faithful $F$-representation of $G$.
Define $K=F(V)^G$ and $K_i=F(V)^{H_i}$.
We obtain group homomorphisms $j:\Gamma_K\to G$ and $j_i:\Gamma_{K_i}\to H_i$.

Each index 2-subgroup $H_i$ of $G$ is the kernel of a character $x_i\in H^1(G,\mathbb F_2)$.
Then $j^*(x_i)\in H^1(K,\mathbb F_2)$ is a group homomorphism from $\Gamma_K$ to $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$.
Lemma \ref{restriction les} and $j$ induce the following commutative diagram with exact rows in each degree $d\geq1$.
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
    H^{d-1}(G,\mathbb F_2)\arrow{r}{\cup x_i}\arrow{d}{j^*} &H^{d}(G,\mathbb F_2)\arrow{r}{\text{res}_i}\arrow{d}{j^*} &H^{d}(H_i,\mathbb F_2)\arrow{d}{j_i^*} \\
    H^{d-1}(K,\mathbb F_2)\arrow{r}{\cup j^*(x_i)} &H^{d}(K,\mathbb F_2)\arrow{r}{\text{res}_i} &H^{d}(K_i,\mathbb F_2)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}

Replace $u$ by some power of $u$ so that $u$ restricts to a negligible element over $F$ in the cohomology of each $H_i$.
Then $\text{res}_i(j^*(u))=j_i^*(\text{res}_i(u))=0$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$.
Since $\text{res}_i(j^*(u))$ is trivial for each $1\leq i\leq n$, exactness of the bottom row implies that $j^*(u)$ is divisible by $j^*(x_i)$ for each $1\leq i\leq n$.
Let $\beta:H^1(G,\mathbb F_2)\to H^2(G,\mathbb F_2)$ be the Bockstein homomorphism, which, in this case, is the squaring map.
Since $G$ is not an elementary abelian 2-group, \cite[Proposition 4]{Se} proves there is some sequence of the $x_i$ for which $\prod\beta(x_i)=\prod x_i^2=0$.
Thus, there is a positive integer $m$ for which $j^*(u)^{2m}$ is divisible by $\prod j^*(x_i)^2=\prod j^*(\beta(x_i))=j^*(\prod\beta(x_i))=0$.
Since $j^*(u)$ is nilpotent in $H^*(K,\mathbb F_2)$, $u\in H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)$ is eventually negligible over $F$.
head: environment

label: proof-theorem-elem-ab
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof-theorem-elem-ab}
Let $E$ be an elementary abelian $p$-subgroup of $G$.
In the case that $F$ is not a formally real field, \cite[Theorem 2.2]{GhermanMerkurjevJPAA} proves that each class of $H^*(G,\mathbb{F}_p)$ and each class of $H^*(E,\mathbb{F}_p)$ is eventually negligible.
For the theorem when $F$ is formally real, the case $p$ odd is also covered by \cite[Theorem 2.2]{GhermanMerkurjevJPAA} since in positive degree every class is eventually negligible.
Thus, the only remaining nontrivial case over a field $F$ that is formally real is $p=2$.
If $p=2$, $F$ is formally real, and $G$ is odd order, $G$ contains no non-trivial elementary abelian 2-subgroups and $H^{>0}(G,\mathbb F_2)$ is trivial.
The result trivially holds.
We are left to prove the case in which $p=2$, $F$ is formally real, and $G$ is even order.

By Lemma \ref{half conjecture}, we need only prove the following.
If $u\in H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)$ restricts to an eventually negligible element in $H^*(E,\mathbb F_2)$ for each elementary abelian 2-subgroup $E\subset G$, then $u$ is eventually negligible.
If the result holds for a Sylow 2-subgroup of $G$, then Lemma \ref{intersection lemma} implies that the result holds for $G$.
We assume without loss of generality that $G$ is a 2-group.

We will proceed by induction on $|G|$.
The base case is the cyclic group of order 2, for which there are no non-trivial negligible classes by \cite[Theorem 4.1]{GhermanMerkurjevJPAA}.
In the inductive step, if $G$ is an elementary abelian 2-group, the result holds by inspection \cite[Theorem 4.1]{GhermanMerkurjevJPAA}.
Lemma \ref{index 2 subgroups} proves the inductive step when $G$ is not elementary abelian.

title: Proof
body_md:
The Sylow 2-subgroup of $D_{2n}$ is isomorphic $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$.
By \cite[Lemma 26.4]{SerreBook}, $I(\mathbb Z / 2\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)$ has trivial negligible cohomology, so $I(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)$ is trivial by Lemma \ref{intersection lemma}.
head: environment

label: dihedralm2
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $n=2\ell$ with $\ell$ odd. Then $|D_{2n}|=4\ell$, and a Sylow $2$-subgroup $E\subset D_{2n}$ is elementary abelian of rank $2$ and has odd index $\ell$.
Choose degree-one generators $a,b\in H^1(E,\mathbb F_2)$ so that, after relabeling if necessary, $\mathrm{res}_E(u)=a$ and $\mathrm{res}_E(v)=b$.
By Lemma \ref{intersection lemma},
\[
I(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)=H^*(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)\cap I(E,\mathbb F_2).
\]
For $E\simeq(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2$, Theorem \ref{negideal} gives
\[
I(E,\mathbb F_2)=\langle ab(a+b)\rangle.
\]
Therefore $I(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)=\langle uv(u+v)\rangle$. Since $u(u+v)+w=0$ in this case, this ideal is also $\langle vw\rangle$.
The ideal $I(E,\mathbb F_2)$ is radical, so its preimage under restriction is radical.
head: environment

label: dihedral even n
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Up to conjugacy, there are three elementary abelian $2$-subgroups of $D_{2n}$, two of which are maximal \cite{unijenaCohomologyFinite}.
Let $E_1,E_2$ denote the two maximal ones of rank 2. 
With respect to generators $u,v,w$ for $H^*(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)$ and generators $x_1,x_2$ for $H^*(E_i,\mathbb F_2)$, \cite{unijenaCohomologyFinite} computes the restriction maps:
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{res}_{E_1}\colon &\quad u \mapsto x_2,\qquad v \mapsto 0,\qquad w \mapsto x_1x_2+x_1^2,\\
\mathrm{res}_{E_2}\colon &\quad u \mapsto 0,\qquad v \mapsto x_2,\qquad w \mapsto x_1x_2+x_1^2.
\end{align*}
By Theorem~\ref{negideal}, the products $uw$ and $vw$ lie in $N(G,\mathbb F_2)$.
We claim
\[
N(G,\mathbb F_2)=\langle uw, vw\rangle.
\]
In the quotient,
\[
H^*(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)/\langle uw,vw\rangle
\simeq \mathbb F_2[u,v,w]/\langle u(u+v),uw,vw\rangle.
\]
It remains to show that no additional non-zero class is eventually negligible.
Let $y\in H^*(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)/\langle uw,vw\rangle$ be a homogeneous element of degree $d>0$.
Indeed, $uw=vw=0$ kills all mixed terms involving $w$, while $u(u+v)=0$ gives $u^2=uv$, so every degree-$d$ monomial in $u$ and $v$ reduces to either $u^d$ or $v^d$.
Using these relations, every such $y$ can be written as
\[
y=\alpha_1 u^d+\alpha_2 v^d+\alpha_3 w^{d/2},
\qquad \alpha_i\in \mathbb F_2.
\]
with $\alpha_3=0$ if $d$ is odd. Under restriction to $E_1$ and $E_2$ this becomes
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{res}_{E_1}(y) &= \alpha_1 x_2^d+\alpha_3 (x_1x_2+x_1^2)^{d/2},\\
\mathrm{res}_{E_2}(y) &= \alpha_2 x_2^d+\alpha_3 (x_1x_2+x_1^2)^{d/2}.
\end{align*}
Assume for contradiction that $y$ is eventually negligible.  By Theorem~\ref{detect on elem ab}, its restriction to each elementary abelian $2$-subgroup is negligible.
By Proposition~\ref{elem ab 2-group vanishing}, for an elementary abelian $2$-group this is equivalent to vanishing upon evaluation at $(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2$.
Evaluate at $(x_1,x_2)=(0,1)$. Then $x_1x_2+x_1^2=0$, so
\[
\mathrm{res}_{E_1}(y)(0,1)=\alpha_1,\qquad \mathrm{res}_{E_2}(y)(0,1)=\alpha_2.
\]
Negligibility forces both to vanish, hence $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0$.

Assume $d$ is even.
Evaluate at $(x_1,x_2)=(1,0)$.
Then $x_1x_2+x_1^2=1$, so
\[
\mathrm{res}_{E_1}(y)(1,0)=\mathrm{res}_{E_2}(y)(1,0)=\alpha_3.
\]
Thus, $\alpha_3=0$, and $y=0$ in $H^*(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)/\langle uw,vw\rangle$.

title: Remark
body_md:
To illustrate the first example of this method concretely, we display the corresponding long exact sequence in Figure \ref{GysinD2n-1}.
In the proofs throughout the rest of the paper, we refer to the diagrams in the Appendix \ref{appendix}.
head: environment

label: prop:uw-and-uw+vw-negligible
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by induction on $n$. For the base case $n=3$, Proposition \ref{dihedral even n} gives
$N(D_8,\mathbb F_2)=\langle uw,vw\rangle.$
Since Theorem \ref{Weylneg} shows that $I(D_8,\mathbb F_2)$ is radical, it follows that $\{uw,\;vw\}\subset I(D_8,\mathbb F_2).$
Alternatively, \cite[Theorem 6.1]{BaekMerkurjev} proves the result.

Now let $n\geq 4$, and suppose inductively that
$u'w'$ and $u'w'+v'w'$
are negligible in $H^*(D_{2^{n-1}},\mathbb F_2)$.

We first prove that $uw+vw$ is negligible in $H^*(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$.
Consider the index-two subgroup $D_{2^{n-1}}\subset D_{2^n}$ generated by $r^2$ and $s$, and choose
the generators $u,v\in H^1(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)=\mathrm{Hom}(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$ by
\[
u(r)=\overline{1},\qquad u(s)=\overline{0},\qquad
v(r)=\overline{0},\qquad v(s)=\overline{1}.
\]
Let $u',v'\in H^1(D_{2^{n-1}},\mathbb F_2)$ be defined analogously on the subgroup generated by $r^2$ and $s$.
Then
\[
\mathrm{res}(u)(r^2)=u(r^2)=u(r+r)=\overline{0},\qquad
\mathrm{res}(u)(s)=u(s)=\overline{0},
\]
so $\mathrm{res}(u)=0$, while
\[
\mathrm{res}(v)(r^2)=v(r^2)=v(r+r)=\overline{0},\qquad
\mathrm{res}(v)(s)=v(s)=\overline{1},
\]
so $\mathrm{res}(v)=v'$. Thus the degree-$1$ restriction map is
\[
\mathrm{res}(u)=0,\qquad \mathrm{res}(v)=v'.
\]
Using this restriction map and the connecting homomorphism given by cup product with $u$, one obtains the long exact sequence displayed in Figure \ref{GysinD2n-1}.
Since restriction is a ring homomorphism, the degree-one computation determines the higher restriction maps appearing in Figure \ref{GysinD2n-1}.

By Figure \ref{GysinD2n-1}, the kernel of
\[
H^3(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)\xrightarrow{\cup u} H^4(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)
\]
is generated by $\{uw+vw,\;u^3+v^3\}.$
By exactness, this kernel is equal to the image of
\[
\mathrm{cor}^3:H^3(D_{2^{n-1}},\mathbb F_2)\to H^3(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2).
\]
 Since $u'w'$ is negligible in $H^*(D_{2^{n-1}},\mathbb F_2)$, Lemma
\ref{lemma:corestriction} implies that the non-zero $\mathrm{cor}^3(u'w')$ is negligible in $H^*(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$.
On the other hand, $u^3+v^3$ and $uw+vw+u^3+v^3$ are not eventually negligible, so $\mathrm{cor}^3(u'w')=uw+vw.$
It follows that $uw+vw$ is negligible in $H^*(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$.

We now prove that $uw$ is negligible.
For this, we use the second description of the degree-one generators,
\[
u(r)=\overline{1},\qquad u(s)=\overline{1},\qquad
v(r)=\overline{0},\qquad v(s)=\overline{1}.
\]
Again, let $u',v'$ denote the corresponding generators of
$H^1(D_{2^{n-1}},\mathbb F_2)$.
Then
\[
\mathrm{res}(u)(r^2)=u(r^2)=u(r+r)=\overline{0},\qquad
\mathrm{res}(u)(s)=u(s)=\overline{1},
\]
so $\mathrm{res}(u)=v'$, and similarly
\[
\mathrm{res}(v)(r^2)=v(r^2)=v(r+r)=\overline{0},\qquad
\mathrm{res}(v)(s)=v(s)=\overline{1},
\]
so $\mathrm{res}(v)=v'$. Consequently,
\[
\mathrm{res}(u+v)=\mathrm{res}(u)+\mathrm{res}(v)=v'+v'=0.
\]
Thus, the degree-one restriction map for this second choice is
\[
\mathrm{res}(u)=v',\qquad \mathrm{res}(v)=v',\qquad \mathrm{res}(u+v)=0.
\]
Using this restriction map and the connecting homomorphism given by cup product with $u+v$, one obtains the long exact sequence in Figure \ref{GysinD2^n(uplusv)}.

Since the relation in the cohomology ring is $u(u+v)=0,$ we have $u^2=uv.$
By Figure \ref{GysinD2^n(uplusv)}, the kernel of
\[
H^3(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)\xrightarrow{\cup (u+v)} H^4(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)
\]
is generated by $\{uw,\;u^3\}.$
By exactness, this kernel is equal to the image of
\[
\mathrm{cor}^3:H^3(D_{2^{n-1}},\mathbb F_2)\to H^3(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, both $u'w'$ and $v'w'$ are negligible in $H^*(D_{2^{n-1}},\mathbb F_2)$, so $\mathrm{cor}^3(u'w')$ and $\mathrm{cor}^3(v'w')$ are negligible in $H^*(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$ by Lemma \ref{lemma:corestriction}.
Moreover, by Proposition \ref{corestriction identity},
$$\mathrm{cor}\big((u')^3\big)=\mathrm{cor}\big(u'(v')^2\big)=\mathrm{cor}(u')u^2=u^3.$$
Hence $u^3$ is the image of $(u')^3$ under corestriction.
Since $u^3$ and $u^3+uw$ are not eventually negligible, the other generator of $\mathrm{Im}(\mathrm{cor}^3)$, namely $uw$, must be the corestriction of a negligible class.
Therefore, $uw$ is negligible in $H^*(D_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$, which completes the induction.

label: dihedralm0
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Write $2n=2^k\ell$, where $k\geq3$ and $\ell$ is odd. Then a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $D_{2n}$ is isomorphic to $D_{2^k}$. Since this subgroup has odd index $\ell$, Lemma \ref{intersection lemma} identifies the negligible ideal of $D_{2n}$ with the intersection of $H^*(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)$ and the negligible ideal of $D_{2^k}$ under restriction. Proposition \ref{prop:uw-and-uw+vw-negligible} gives $I(D_{2^k},\mathbb F_2)=\langle uw,vw\rangle$, so $I(D_{2n},\mathbb F_2)=\langle uw,vw\rangle$. Thus the negligible ideal of $D_{2n}$ is radical.
head: environment

label: cyclic-2-eventually-negligible
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{cyclic-2-eventually-negligible}
For $n\geq 2$, $N(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)=\langle x\rangle$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The unique elementary abelian $2$-subgroup of $\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z$ is $E\simeq \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$, with $H^*(E,\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[t]$ where $\deg t=1$.
The restriction map on generators is $$\mathrm{res}(x)=0,\qquad \mathrm{res}(y)=t^2.$$
Since $H^*(E,\mathbb F_2)$ is a polynomial ring on a single degree-one generator, Theorem~\ref{negideal} gives $I(E,\mathbb F_2)=0$, so no non-zero homogeneous class of $H^*(E,\mathbb F_2)$ is negligible. By Theorem~\ref{detect on elem ab}, a class of $H^*(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)$ is eventually negligible if and only if it restricts to zero on $E$. Since $\mathrm{res}(x)=0$ while $\mathrm{res}(y^r)=t^{2r}\ne 0$ for $r\geq 1$, the kernel of $\mathrm{res}$ is exactly $\langle x\rangle$, hence $N(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)=\langle x\rangle$.
head: environment

label: cyclic-2-xy-negligible
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{cyclic-2-xy-negligible}
The class $xy$ is negligible in $H^*(\mathbb Z/{2^n}\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $D_{2^{n+1}}=\langle r,s\rangle$ be the dihedral group containing the cyclic subgroup $\langle r\rangle\simeq \mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z$.
Use the standard generators $u,v,w\in H^*(D_{2^{n+1}},\mathbb F_2)$, and choose them so that $\langle r\rangle=\ker(v)$. Let $x\in H^1(\langle r\rangle,\mathbb F_2)$ and $y\in H^2(\langle r\rangle,\mathbb F_2)$ be the standard generators of
\[
H^*(\langle r\rangle,\mathbb F_2)\cong \mathbb F_2[x,y]/\langle x^2\rangle.
\]
On degree-one generators, restriction gives
\[
\mathrm{res}(u)=x,\qquad \mathrm{res}(v)=0.
\]
The degree-two lift in the same restriction computation gives $\mathrm{res}(w)=y$, hence
\[
\mathrm{res}(uw)=xy.
\]
By Proposition \ref{prop:uw-and-uw+vw-negligible}, the class $uw$ is negligible in $H^*(D_{2^{n+1}},\mathbb F_2)$. Lemma \ref{half conjecture} then implies that its restriction $xy$ is negligible in $H^*(\langle r\rangle,\mathbb F_2)$.
head: environment

label: cyclic-2-negligible
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cyclic-2-negligible}
For $n\geq 2$, $I(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)=\langle xy\rangle$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every negligible class is eventually negligible, so by Proposition~\ref{cyclic-2-eventually-negligible},
\[
I(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)\subseteq N(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)=\langle x\rangle.
\]
Using $x^2=0$, the homogeneous elements of $\langle x\rangle$ are exactly the classes $\alpha\, xy^k$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb F_2$ and $k\geq 0$, of degree $2k+1$. Let $z\in I(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)$ be a non-zero homogeneous element, so $z=xy^k$ for some $k\geq 0$. The case $k=0$ would give the degree-one class $z=x$, which is not negligible by Theorem~\ref{nonneg-low-degree}. Hence $k\geq 1$ and $z=xy\cdot y^{k-1}\in\langle xy\rangle$. This proves $I(\mathbb Z/2^n\mathbb Z,\mathbb F_2)\subseteq\langle xy\rangle$. The reverse inclusion follows from Proposition~\ref{cyclic-2-xy-negligible}.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
For $\ell_i \geq 2$,
\[H^*\!\left(\mathbb{Z}/2^{\ell_i}\mathbb{Z},\,\mathbb F_2\right)\cong\mathbb F_2[x_i,y_i]/\langle x_i^2\rangle.\]
head: environment

label: 2x4
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The class $x_j$ restricts to zero on $E_{\max}$. The class
$x_i^2x_{i'}+x_ix_{i'}^2$ restricts to a generator of
$I(E_{\max},\mathbb F_2)$ and is therefore eventually negligible. The third generator restricts to
\[
x_j^2x_{j'}^4+x_{j'}^2x_j^4=(x_jx_{j'}^2+x_j^2x_{j'})^2,
\]
and the fourth restricts to $$x_i x_j^2 (x_i^2+x_j^2)=(x_ix_j^2+x_i^2x_j)\cdot x_j(x_i+x_j).$$
By Theorem~\ref{negideal}, both of these images lie in $I(E,\mathbb F_2)$, so by Theorem ~\ref{detect on elem ab}, the generators are eventually negligible.
head: environment

label: lem2x4
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{lem2x4}
    Let $G$ be a finite abelian $2$-group, $x_i$ be a degree one generator of $H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)$, and $y_j$ a degree two generator of $H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)$.
    Then for all $k\geq 3$ and $\ell\geq1$, we have 
    $$x_i^{k}y_j^{\ell} = x_i^{k+2(\ell-1)}y_j$$ in the quotient $H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)/N(G,\mathbb F_2)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $x_i y_j(x_i^2 + y_j) \in N(G, \mathbb F_2)$ by Proposition \ref{2x4}, this element must map to zero in the quotient.
    With a slight abuse of notation, we can say in the quotient
    $$x_i y_j(x_i^2 + y_j) = x_i^3y_j + x_i y_j^2 = 0.$$
    Since the coefficients lie in $\mathbb F_2$, this gives  $$x_i^3y_j=x_iy_j^2.$$
    Now write 
    \[
    x_i^k y_j^{\ell}
    =x_i^{k-1}x_i y_j^{\ell-2}y_j^2
    =x_i^{k-1}y_j^{\ell-2}x_i^{3}y_j
    =x_i^{k+2}y_j^{\ell-1}.
    \]
    By induction, we obtain 
    \[
    x_i^k y_j^{\ell}
    = x_i^{k+2(\ell-1)}y_j. \qedhere
    \]
head: environment

label: lem32
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The restriction maps are either the identity or the zero map. Thus, by Theorem \ref{negideal}, $x_i^2x_j + x_ix_j^2$ are in the eventually negligible ideal, and
    $$ x_i^2 x_j + x_ix_j^2 = 0\implies  x_i^2x_j = x_ix_j^2\mod 2.$$
    Then observe
    $$x_i^kx_j^\ell=x_i^{k - 1}x_j^{\ell - 2} (x_i x_j^2) = x_i^{k - 1}x_j^{\ell - 2} (x_i^2 x_j) = x_i^{k + 1}x_j^{\ell - 1}.$$
    The result follows by induction.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian 2-group that is neither cyclic nor elementary abelian.
    With indices as in Equation (\ref{elem ab indices}),
    $$N(G,\mathbb F_2)  = \langle x_j, x_i^2x_{i'} + x_ix_{i'}^2, y_j^2y_{j'} + y_jy_{j'}^2, x_iy_j(x_i^2 + y_j)\rangle.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
$$ J=\langle x_j,\ x_i^2x_{i'}+x_ix_{i'}^2,\ y_j^2y_{j'}+y_jy_{j'}^2,\ x_iy_j(x_i^2+y_j)\rangle,$$
where the indices have the same ranges as in the statement. Proposition~\ref{2x4} gives $J\subseteq N(G,\mathbb F_2)$, so it remains to prove the reverse inclusion. Since $E_{\max}$ is the unique maximal elementary abelian $2$-subgroup of $G$, every elementary abelian $2$-subgroup is contained in $E_{\max}$. Hence, by Corollary~\ref{quillen-venkov} and Lemma~\ref{half conjecture}, $N(G,\mathbb F_2)=\operatorname{res}^{-1}(I(E_{\max},\mathbb F_2))$. It is therefore enough to prove that the induced map
$$\overline{\operatorname{res}}\colon H^*(G,\mathbb F_2)/J
\longrightarrow H^*(E_{\max},\mathbb F_2)/I(E_{\max},\mathbb F_2)$$
is injective. Write $L=\{1,\dots,\ell\}$ and $H=\{\ell+1,\dots,m\}$, and argue degree by degree. The degree-zero case is immediate, so fix $d>0$. In the quotient by $J$, the generators $x_j$ for $j\in H$ vanish. Thus every degree-$d$ monomial is represented by $M=\prod_{i\in S_x}x_i^{a_i}\prod_{j\in S_y}y_j^{b_j}$, where $S_x\subseteq L$, $S_y\subseteq H$, and $a_i,b_j\geq1$. The defining relations of $J$ imply, for positive integers $a,b$,
$$ x_i^ax_{i'}^b=x_i^{a+b-1}x_{i'},\qquad
y_j^ay_{j'}^b=y_j^{a+b-1}y_{j'},\qquad
x_i^ay_j^b=x_i^{a+2(b-1)}y_j. $$

Suppose first that $S_x\neq\varnothing$, and let $i_0$ be its smallest element. Repeatedly applying these relations reduces $M$ to the canonical monomial $M_{S_x,S_y}^{(d)}=x_{i_0}^{\,d-|S_x|-2|S_y|+1}\prod_{i\in S_x\setminus\{i_0\}}x_i\prod_{j\in S_y}y_j$. The exponent of $x_{i_0}$ is positive because $d\geq |S_x|+2|S_y|$. If $S_x=\varnothing$, then $S_y\neq\varnothing$ and $d$ is even. Writing $j_0$ for the smallest element of $S_y$, the $y$-relations reduce $M$ to $M_{\varnothing,S_y}^{(d)}=y_{j_0}^{\,d/2-|S_y|+1}\prod_{j\in S_y\setminus\{j_0\}}y_j$. Consequently, every homogeneous $f\in H^d(G,\mathbb F_2)/J$ can be written as $f=\sum_{S_x,S_y}c_{S_x,S_y}M_{S_x,S_y}^{(d)}$, where $c_{S_x,S_y}\in\mathbb F_2$ and each pair $(S_x,S_y)$ occurs at most once. Indeed, monomials with the same support reduce to the same canonical monomial, after which their coefficients are combined in $\mathbb F_2$. Let $f\neq0$, and choose a pair $(S_x,S_y)$ with $c_{S_x,S_y}=1$ such that $S=S_x\cup S_y$ is minimal under inclusion among the supports with non-zero coefficient. Choose polynomial generators $t_1,\dots,t_m$ for $H^*(E_{\max},\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2[t_1,\dots,t_m]$ so that $\operatorname{res}(x_i)=t_i$ for $i\in L$ and $\operatorname{res}(y_j)=t_j^2$ for $j\in H$. Let $\mathbf 1_S\in\mathbb F_2^m$ have $r$-th coordinate equal to $1$ when $r\in S$ and $0$ otherwise. A canonical monomial with support $T$ evaluates at $\mathbf 1_S$ to $1$ exactly when $T\subseteq S$. By minimality, no proper subset of $S$ occurs with non-zero coefficient, and by construction there is only one canonical monomial with support $S$. Thus $\operatorname{res}(f)(\mathbf 1_S)=1$. By Proposition~\ref{elem ab 2-group vanishing}, $\operatorname{res}(f)$ is not negligible, so $\overline{\operatorname{res}}(f)\neq0$. Therefore $\overline{\operatorname{res}}$ is injective and $N(G,\mathbb F_2)\subseteq J$. Together with Proposition~\ref{2x4}, this proves $N(G,\mathbb F_2)=J$.

label: Q8
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is obtained by chasing the Gysin long exact sequences in Figures~\ref{Q16resC8}--\ref{Q32resQ16-2}.
In each case the chosen index-two subgroup is the kernel of the indicated degree-one character, so the connecting maps are cup product with that character, and exactness identifies the kernel of this cup-product map with the image of the corresponding corestriction map.
Figure~\ref{Q16resC8} shows that, in the base case $Q_{16}$, the negligible class $xy\in H^3(C_8,\mathbb F_2)$ corestricts to $a^3=b^3$, while Figures~\ref{Q16resQ8-1} and~\ref{Q16resQ8-2} show that $bc$ and $ac$ are likewise obtained by corestricting negligible classes from the relevant index-two subgroups.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:corestriction} therefore gives $a^3,ac,bc\in I(Q_{16},\mathbb F_2)$.
The same diagram chase in Figures~\ref{Q32resC16}--\ref{Q32resQ16-2} proves the inductive step.
Figure~\ref{Q32resC16} gives $a^3=b^3$, and Figures~\ref{Q32resQ16-1} and~\ref{Q32resQ16-2} give $ac$ and $bc$.
Hence $\langle a^3,ac,bc\rangle\subseteq I(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$.




For the reverse inclusion, we first compute the eventually negligible ideal. We claim that
$N(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)=\langle a,b\rangle$ for $n\geq 4$. Recall that
$$ H^*(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)
= \mathbb F_2[a,b,c]/\langle ab,\ a^3+b^3\rangle, \quad
\deg(a)=\deg(b)=1,\quad \deg(c)=4. $$
The group $Q_{2^n}$ has a unique subgroup of order $2$, namely
$C=\langle z\rangle\cong C_2$, where $z=i^{2^{n-2}}$.
Thus, $C$ is the only non-trivial elementary abelian $2$-subgroup of $Q_{2^n}$.
By Corollary~\ref{quillen-venkov}, a class $u\in H^*(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$ is eventually negligible if and only if $\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(u)$ is negligible.
Since $H^*(C,\mathbb F_2)\cong \mathbb F_2[t]$, with $\deg(t)=1$, and $I(C,\mathbb F_2)=0$ by Theorem~\ref{negideal}, this gives
$$ u\in N(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2) \iff\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(u)=0.$$
Hence, $N(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)=\ker(\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}})$. We now compute this kernel.
Since $a$ and $b$ are degree-one classes, they are homomorphisms $Q_{2^n}\to \mathbb F_2$.
The element $z=i^{2^{n-2}}$ is an even power of $i$, so every degree-one class vanishes on $z$.
Hence, $\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(a)=\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(b)=0$, so $\langle a,b\rangle\subseteq \ker(\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}})$.
Further, since $\deg(c)=4$, we have $\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(c)\in H^4(C,\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2\cdot t^4$, so $\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(c)$ is either $0$ or $t^4$.
If it were $0$, then $c$ would restrict trivially to every elementary abelian $2$-subgroup of
$Q_{2^n}$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:quillen-venkov-nilpotence} would imply
that $c$ is nilpotent. But
$$ H^*(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)/\langle a,b\rangle\cong \mathbb F_2[c],$$
so no positive power of $c$ is zero. Thus $\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(c)\neq 0$,
and hence $\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}}(c)=t^4$. After quotienting by
$\langle a,b\rangle$, the induced map is
$$
\mathbb F_2[c]\to \mathbb F_2[t],
\qquad
c\mapsto t^4,
$$
which is injective. Therefore
$\ker(\mathrm{res}_C^{Q_{2^n}})=\langle a,b\rangle$, and hence
$$
N(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)=\langle a,b\rangle.
$$

Let $u\in I(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$ be homogeneous.
Since every negligible class is eventually negligible, $u\in N(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)=\langle a,b\rangle$.
If $\deg(u)=1$ or $\deg(u)=2$, then $u=0$ by Theorem~\ref{nonneg-low-degree}.
Hence $u\in\langle a^3,ac,bc\rangle$ in
degrees $0,1,$ and $2$.
Assume now that $\deg(u)\geq 3$.
In $H^*(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)$ we have
$a^3=b^3$, and hence
$$ a^4=a(a^3)=a(b^3)=(ab)b^2=0, \qquad b^4=b(b^3)=b(a^3)=(ab)a^2=0. $$
Every homogeneous element of $\langle a,b\rangle$ is a sum of monomials which contain a factor of $a$ or $b$.
If such a monomial has degree at
least $3$ and contains no factor of $c$, then the relations above imply that it is a multiple of $a^3=b^3$.
If it contains a factor of $c$, then, since it also contains a factor of $a$ or $b$, it is a multiple of $ac$ or $bc$.
Therefore,
$$ \langle a,b\rangle\cap H^{\geq 3}(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)
\subseteq \langle a^3,ac,bc\rangle, $$
and $u\in\langle a^3,ac,bc\rangle$.
Since every homogeneous negligible class lies in $\langle a^3,ac,bc\rangle$ and the negligible ideal is graded,
we obtain
$$ I(Q_{2^n},\mathbb F_2)\subseteq \langle  a^3,ac,bc\rangle,$$
proving the reverse inclusion.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In what follows, we use the notation $H_3$ and $H_4$ for the finite Coxeter
groups of types $H_3$ and $H_4$, respectively. Strictly speaking, $H_3$ and
$H_4$ denote Coxeter types or Coxeter diagrams, and the corresponding finite
Coxeter groups are generated by the simple reflections attached to those
diagrams. We follow the common convention of writing $H_3$ and $H_4$ for the
groups themselves.
head: environment

label: radicality-h3
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Coxeter group of type $H_3$ is isomorphic to $ A_5\times \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ \cite[Section~6]{KOCA2006441}. Let
$V\leq A_5$ be the subgroup $$ V=  \{1,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}.$$
Then $V$ is a Klein four group, so
$V\cong \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\times \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z.$
Moreover, since $|A_5|=60$, the subgroup $V$ is a Sylow-$2$ subgroup of $A_5$. Choose an isomorphism $H_3\cong A_5\times \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z,$ and let $E\leq H_3$ be the subgroup corresponding to $ V\times \mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z.$ Then $ E\cong(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^3 $ and $[H_3:E]=|H_3|/|E|= 120/8=15.$ In particular, $[H_3:E]$ is prime to $2$. Since $E$ is elementary abelian,
Theorem~\ref{negideal} and Proposition~\ref{elem ab 2-group vanishing} imply that $I(E,\mathbb F_2)$ is radical.
Now one can apply Lemma~\ref{intersection lemma} to the inclusion
$E\leq H_3$, and restriction gives an injection
$$ \mathrm{res}_{E}^{H_3}: H^\ast(H_3,\mathbb F_2) \hookrightarrow H^\ast(E,\mathbb F_2).$$
Identifying $H^\ast(H_3,\mathbb F_2)$ with its image under restriction, Lemma~\ref{intersection lemma} gives
$$I(H_3,\mathbb F_2) =H^\ast(H_3,\mathbb F_2)\cap I(E,\mathbb F_2).$$

Now let $x\in H^\ast(H_3,\mathbb F_2)$ and suppose that
$ x^m\in I(H_3,\mathbb F_2)$ for some $m\geq 1$. Restricting to $E$, we get $$ \mathrm{res}_{E}^{H_3}(x)^m  =\mathrm{res}_{E}^{H_3}(x^m) \in I(E,\mathbb F_2).$$
Since $I(E,\mathbb F_2)$ is radical, it follows that
$\mathrm{res}_{E}^{H_3}(x)\in I(E,\mathbb F_2). $
But $\mathrm{res}_{E}^{H_3}(x)$ also lies in the image of
$H^\ast(H_3,\mathbb F_2)$ inside $H^\ast(E,\mathbb F_2)$. Hence, by the intersection formula, $ x\in I(H_3,\mathbb F_2). $
Therefore $I(H_3,\mathbb F_2)$ is radical.
head: environment

label: radicality-h4
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{radicality-h4}
The mod-$2$ negligible ideal $I(H_4,\mathbb F_2)$ over $\mathbb Q$ is radical.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Section~5]{KOCA2006441}, the Coxeter group of type $H_4$ contains
a subgroup of the form
$
        W(D_4)\rtimes \mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z.
$
In particular, $H_4$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $W(D_4)$, the Weyl
group of type $D_4$. Here $D_4$ denotes the Coxeter type and $W(D_4)$ its Weyl group. This
should not be confused with the notation used above for dihedral groups. The Weyl group $W(D_4)$ has order $ |W(D_4)|=192,$ and the Coxeter group $H_4$ has order $|H_4|=14400.$ Since $[H_4:W(D_4)] = 14400/192 =75,$ Lemma~\ref{intersection lemma} gives the inclusion
$ W(D_4)\leq H_4.$ Thus restriction gives an injection
$$\mathrm{res}_{W(D_4)}^{H_4}: H^\ast(H_4,\mathbb F_2)
\hookrightarrow H^\ast(W(D_4),\mathbb F_2),$$
and, after identifying $H^\ast(H_4,\mathbb F_2)$ with its image under restriction, $$ I(H_4,\mathbb F_2)= H^\ast(H_4,\mathbb F_2)\cap I(W(D_4),\mathbb F_2).$$
Since $W(D_4)$ is a Weyl group, Theorem~\ref{Weylneg} implies that
$I(W(D_4),\mathbb F_2)$ is radical. Now let $x\in H^\ast(H_4,\mathbb F_2)$ and suppose that $x^m\in I(H_4,\mathbb F_2)$ for some $m\geq 1$. Restricting to $W(D_4)$,
we get $$ \mathrm{res}_{W(D_4)}^{H_4}(x)^m =\mathrm{res}_{W(D_4)}^{H_4}(x^m)\in I(W(D_4),\mathbb F_2).$$
Since $I(W(D_4),\mathbb F_2)$ is radical, it follows that
$\mathrm{res}_{W(D_4)}^{H_4}(x)\in I(W(D_4),\mathbb F_2).$
But $\mathrm{res}_{W(D_4)}^{H_4}(x)$ also lies in the image of
$H^\ast(H_4,\mathbb F_2)$ inside $H^\ast(W(D_4),\mathbb F_2)$. Hence, by
the intersection formula,
$x\in I(H_4,\mathbb F_2).$
Therefore $I(H_4,\mathbb F_2)$ is radical.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{Weylneg}, all Weyl groups have radical mod-$2$ negligible ideal over
$\mathbb Q$. By the classification of finite irreducible Coxeter groups, the
irreducible Coxeter groups which are not Weyl groups are the dihedral groups
$I_2(m)$ and the exceptional noncrystallographic groups $H_3$ and $H_4$.
The dihedral cases were proved in Section~\ref{dihedral}, the $H_3$ case was proved in
Lemma~\ref{radicality-h3}, and the $H_4$ case is Lemma~\ref{radicality-h4}. Hence the
result holds for all finite irreducible Coxeter groups.
